4: Calling a large model through an API is the least hassle: send the request, the model computes and returns the result, and the user neither buys a GPU nor maintains the underlying environment.
5: But the API route has limits you cannot avoid, mainly in these areas:
6: Data security: core documents, customer privacy and internal business data cannot simply be sent to a third-party public cloud.
7: Offline use: production environments such as private networks or dedicated lines may not be able to reach the internet at all.
8: Cost control: when the call volume is large and steady, running your own server is usually cheaper overall than paying per token forever.
9: So if the business involves sensitive data, requires fully offline operation or has a high call volume, local deployment is the better fit.
11: Ollama is one of the more comfortable tools available today: it packages model download, local management and the API service together. You do not have to write code to load a model; a couple of commands start it.
12: Whether a model runs smoothly locally depends a lot on the computer's hardware. Ollama supports the common hardware platforms well, including Windows, Linux and macOS. Whether it is a plain CPU, a GPU, or a Mac with Apple Silicon, all can run models.
13: Running on CPU: even without a discrete GPU, a computer can run models on its CPU. Large-model inference needs a lot of computation, so generation on a CPU is usually slow, which suits smaller models or scenarios that do not demand fast responses.
14: Running on GPU: this is the most common way to run large models today. GPUs have strong parallel computing ability and noticeably speed up generation. The bigger the model, the more VRAM it usually needs, so when choosing a model you have to check the GPU has enough VRAM.
15: Running on Apple Silicon: Apple's M-series chips use a unified memory design, so CPU and GPU share the same memory. For Mac users, a device with 32 GB, 64 GB or more of unified memory can try running some larger quantized models.
